title: Responsible artificial intelligence governance: A review and research framework
explain_beginner: AI is spreading quickly through workplaces, and many groups have written lists of ethical rules for it. The problem is that these lists of principles do not tell organizations how to actually put them into daily practice. This paper reviewed many existing studies on responsible AI and found that the research is scattered and unclear. The authors pulled it together and built a framework that describes responsible AI governance as three kinds of practices: structural, relational, and procedural. This matters because it gives organizations a clearer way to think about turning ethical promises about AI into real actions.
explain_business: Many organizations have adopted responsible AI principles, but principles alone do not ensure that AI systems are designed, run, monitored, and evaluated responsibly. This review shows that guidance on turning principles into practice is limited and fragmented. The authors propose a framework that treats responsible AI governance as structural, relational, and procedural practices, along with what drives them and what they affect. For executives, this means governance should be judged by concrete practices rather than stated values. It informs decisions about how to organize oversight, assign responsibilities, and set processes for AI, and it can shape audit and accountability questions.
explain_practitioner: This is a scoping review that synthesizes empirical work on responsible AI and its underlying principles. The authors separate responsible AI principles from responsible AI governance, then critically analyze existing studies to surface their hidden assumptions. From this synthesis they define responsible AI governance as a set of structural, relational, and procedural practices, and they build a conceptual framework covering those practices, their antecedents, and their effects. The key contribution is a clearer conceptual boundary between principles and operational governance, plus a research agenda identifying gaps for future work in the information systems field.
